Dual Exam: Controlled Evaluation of Multimodal Agents and World Models

Zhefan Rao, Meng Chu, Xuan Zhang, Jingfan Chen, Guohao Cai, Runyi Li, Shiyi Du, Ning Lu, Xu Huang, Zhixuan Chen, Feng Nie, Harold Haodong Chen, Hanwen Wang, Wen-Jie Shu, Yajing Bai, Xianfeng Wu, Xuanhua He, Shuhan Guo, Ziyue Ma, Ruichuan An, Long Bai, Miaosen Chai, Wenhao Chai, Jingye Chen, Qi Chen, Xuhang Chen, Wei Chow, Minghao Fu, Yunhao Gou, Haokun Gui, Dong Huang, Wei Huang, Zi Cheng Huang, Haibo Jin, Lingdong Kong, Leung Chun Ho, Tianqin Li, Yanheng Li, Jiayuan Liu, Jiyang Liu, Mingyu Liu, Shaoteng Liu, Xiaocheng Lu, Yawen Luo, Zeyu Qin, Tiancheng Shen, Yueqi Song, Zhaolong Su, Hengkai Tan, Tianhao Tang, Yiran Tao, Juncheng Wang, Qinghe Wang, Shangshang Wang, Yingying Wang, Fang Wu, Tiange Xiang, Qiushi Yang, Weicai Ye, Weichen Yu, Jiarui Zhang, Jize Zhang, Liuzhou Zhang, Renrui Zhang, Sheng Zhang, Wenhu Zhang, Junru Zhao, Lingting Zhu, Yuxin Zuo, Yutong Bai, Long Chen, Yang Deng, Ziqi Huang, Yeying Jin, Weijia Li, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Quande Liu, See-Kiong Ng, Hongliang Ren, Hongru Wang, Shujun Wang, Qifeng Chen, Haoxuan Che The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology National University of Singapore The Hong Kong Polytechnic University The University of Tokyo Carnegie Mellon University University of California, Berkeley University of Central Florida University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill The Chinese University of Hong Kong University of Chicago Princeton University Johns Hopkins University University of Cambridge University of California, San Diego The University of Hong Kong City University of Hong Kong University of California, Merced Cornell University Massachusetts Institute of Technology University of Southern California Stanford University University of Maryland, College Park Singapore Management University Nanyang Technological University University of Oxford University of Edinburgh XGEN Labs ††thanks: Corresponding author.
Abstract

World Models (WMs) can support Multimodal Agents (MAs) through simulated experience and action-conditioned predictions, while MA interaction trajectories can provide feedback for refining WMs. Assessing this potential relationship requires evidence about both components. A pilot study of one MA–WM pairing on 150 cases across ten scenarios illustrates why coupled outcomes alone are insufficient for diagnosing failure. We introduce Dual Exam, a framework that evaluates MAs under a fixed environment response mechanism and WMs under fixed action interventions. The Agent evaluation compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains. The World Model evaluation comprises 400 cases across eight scenarios, with 50 cases per scenario; 15 of 16 configurations cover all eight scenarios, and one covers six. GPT 6 Astra attains the highest Agent Index of 31.3 under the selected case-count weights, while GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall scores at 21.7. These track-specific scores use different tasks and metrics and are not directly comparable. Agent strengths remain category-specific, and the aggregate ordering depends on the domain mixture. The evaluations characterize task-specific execution and state-transition performance. They provide a basis for studying reliable MA–WM interaction, while whether these capabilities predict coupled performance or sustained reciprocal improvement remains to be tested.

1 Introduction

World Models (WMs) and Multimodal Agents (MAs) can improve each other in complementary ways. WMs support MAs through simulated experience and action-conditioned predictions (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025), while MA interaction trajectories provide feedback for refining WMs (Zhang et al., 2026b; Yu et al., 2026). Recent work has coupled the two in specific settings (Fang et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). For example, a web agent can use a world model to anticipate candidate clicks, while its trajectories provide data for model refinement (Fang et al., 2025). Broader multimodal interaction requires both effective action selection and faithful responses to those actions. We assess these complementary requirements across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains (Chu et al., 2026). Our focus is task-specific component performance; the relationship between these measurements and gains from joint training requires separate validation.

However, reciprocal improvement requires both MAs and WMs to remain reliable over repeated interaction. MAs still struggle with visual grounding, action sequencing, and sustained task completion (Xie et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026). WMs also face challenges in memory consistency and action control (Ye et al., 2026b). Visual fidelity or state similarity alone does not guarantee improved planning or successful task completion (Shang et al., 2026a; Huang et al., 2026). These weaknesses become more apparent when MAs and WMs are coupled. The output of one repeatedly becomes the input to the other. WM-based simulation can improve planning (Gu et al., 2025), but the planning benefits depend on behavioral coverage, environment complexity, and whether the MA can use the predicted outcomes (Li et al., 2025b; Qian et al., 2026a). Model bias may also accumulate over repeated rollouts (Janner et al., 2019). End-to-end performance can show that the coupled system fails, but not why. Failures may come from MA decisions, WM responses, or their interaction. A component-level evaluation is therefore needed to characterize the capabilities that end-to-end outcomes alone cannot reveal.

Our preliminary study tests one MA–WM pairing on 150 cases across ten scenarios, with 0% task success under the stated protocol (Section 2.1). The trajectories reveal state discrepancies and limited responses, but do not identify which component caused each failure. This motivates Dual Exam: controlled, separate assessments of MAs and WMs rather than causal attribution from coupled outcomes.

We instantiate Dual Exam across four representative domains: physical, digital, social, and scientific. The two tracks share specification-based verification, assessing recorded evidence against explicit goals and state constraints while retaining track-specific cases and metrics. The Agent evaluation compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items organized into 15 reporting categories. The World Model evaluation contains 400 cases across eight scenarios, with 50 cases per scenario and configuration-specific coverage reported in the results. GPT 6 Astra attains the highest Agent Index of 31.3 under the configured case-count weights. GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall scores at 21.7; 15 of the 16 WM configurations cover all eight scenarios, while Seedance 2.5 is reported separately on six. Performance varies substantially across task categories, and illustrative trajectories distinguish locally plausible behavior from satisfaction of complete task requirements. These measurements characterize the evaluated model–harness configurations under their recorded task specifications; execution settings are not fully matched across configurations. Whether their profiles predict coupled success or improvement through joint training remains an empirical question.

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce Dual Exam, a framework for separate, controlled evaluation of Multimodal Agents and World Models. Both tracks verify recorded evidence against task specifications, using fixed environment response mechanisms for Agents and fixed interventions for World Models.

  • •

    We compare 10 Agent configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories across four domains, and organize the World Model evaluation into 400 cases across eight scenarios. The results provide complementary task and scenario profiles, with explicit aggregation rules and configuration-specific coverage.

  • •

    We provide a 150-case pilot of one MA–WM pairing, together with trajectory audits and a packing example, to illustrate the diagnostic limits of coupled outcomes and motivate the separate evaluations.

2 Dual Exam

We first present a preliminary study of coupled MA–WM interaction to motivate the design of Dual Exam. The framework evaluates Agents under fixed reference environment responses and World Models under fixed action interventions. Both tracks assess task-relevant behavior against specified goals and constraints, while retaining track-specific cases, interaction protocols, and verification procedures. The two tracks need not use one-to-one matched episodes. Evaluation relies on recorded execution evidence rather than self-reported completion. Across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains, Dual Exam comprises 1,088 Agent evaluation items and 400 World Model cases.

Figure 3 summarizes the inventory by domain and reporting category.

2.1 Preliminary Study: Motivation for Dual Exam

As a pilot study, we evaluate GPT-5.6 Sol with Seedance 2.5 on 150 cases across ten scenarios, with 15 cases per scenario. Each case has one attempt of at most 20 interaction steps, with no episode-level retries. Initialization and technical failures are excluded from the 150 cases and the task-success denominator. Table 1 reports a retrospective trajectory audit; Appendix D details the protocol.

World State Consistency measures preservation of task-relevant identity and state and realization of requested action effects, averaging supported checks over applicable checks, then over steps and cases. Agent Corrective Response measures eligible visible discrepancies receiving targeted verification, repositioning, or correction within two actions; it measures response behavior, not successful repair. Task Success requires satisfying the full goal and all constraints. Scenario rates are case-averaged. Overall is recomputed as the unweighted mean of the ten displayed scenario rates, Overall=110​∑s=110rs\mathrm{Overall}=\frac{1}{10}\sum_{s=1}^{10}r_{s}, giving 26.6%, 9.2%, and 0.0% after rounding to one decimal place.

The packing rollout illustrates the gap between issuing task commands and meeting task requirements (Figure 2(b)). Three items must be packed into the same blue backpack and carried to the entryway for inspection. Commands continue despite unconfirmed acquisition, and later packing and carrying use a smaller blue pouch, violating the same-backpack requirement. Six selected frames accompany curves over all 14 steps, ending at 0.316 (6/19 state checks) and 0.286 (2/7 response events). Both responses are navigation retries; none of the four identity discrepancies receives a targeted response.

Unlike the table’s audit, the single-case state score excludes unknown checks. Its curves accumulate deductions from an assigned unit baseline using fixed full-trajectory denominators. Their decline follows from this definition, not measured monotonic capability degradation; they are retrospective diagnostics rather than isolated model scores. Appendix D gives the scoring details and limitations.

The pilot motivates a diagnostic question: how does each component perform when the other side is controlled? Dual Exam holds a fixed reference environment response mechanism fixed to test MAs and fixes action interventions to test WMs against specified goals and constraints (Figure 2(c)). These tests measure role-specific performance rather than retrospectively assigning causes to the pilot failures. Table 2 compares this scope with existing benchmarks.

Research questions.

We ask (RQ1) how Agent task performance varies when the response mechanism is fixed, and (RQ2) how World Models realize prescribed actions while preserving task-relevant state. The pilot motivates these questions; it is not a third, matched factorial experiment. Our four domains provide diverse operational settings, not a complete or orthogonal taxonomy of intelligence. The reporting categories organize tasks and results rather than define independent latent abilities; each task is scored against verifiable outcomes and constraints. The full inventory appears in Table 5.

2.2 Dual Examination Framework

Reliable MA–WM interaction requires both effective action selection and faithful action-conditioned state evolution. An Agent must choose actions that advance the task, while a WM must realize their consequences and preserve task-relevant state. These requirements are interdependent in coupled rollouts: WM outputs inform subsequent MA decisions, and MA actions determine the transitions the WM must generate. End-to-end outcomes therefore reflect both components and their interaction. Dual Exam examines these complementary requirements through two controlled evaluation tracks. The Agent track fixes the environment response mechanism to assess action selection and task completion, while the World Model track fixes action interventions to assess the resulting state evolution. Together, the tracks characterize capability gaps on both sides of the interaction loop. Specifically, the Agent track evaluates a candidate AθA_{\theta} against a fixed reference environment response process:

at∼Aθ​(ht),ot+1∗=𝒯∗​(st,at),a_{t}\sim A_{\theta}(h_{t}),\qquad o_{t+1}^{*}=\mathcal{T}^{*}(s_{t},a_{t}),

where sts_{t} is the reference environment state, hth_{t} is the observation–action history available to the Agent, and ot+1∗o_{t+1}^{*} is the returned reference observation. 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*} denotes the fixed response mechanism, including observation generation; it need not expose the underlying state to the Agent. The Agent is responsible for action selection, verification, recovery, and task completion. The World Model track instead fixes a specification-defined intervention sequence a1:T∗a_{1:T}^{*} and evaluates the resulting observations:

o^t+1=Mϕ​(s^t,at∗).\hat{o}_{t+1}=M_{\phi}(\hat{s}_{t},a_{t}^{*}).

Here, s^t\hat{s}_{t} denotes the generated context carried forward by the WM interface, rather than an observed ground-truth state, and o^t+1\hat{o}_{t+1} is its next generated observation. The superscript ∗* identifies reference inputs or responses. Holding a mechanism fixed controls its variation across candidates; it does not certify its correctness. Appendix C distinguishes recorded validation evidence from unresolved reliability checks. Both tracks assess task-relevant behavior against specified goals and constraints, while retaining track-specific cases, interaction protocols, and verification procedures. Table 2 compares this scope with representative Agent and World Model benchmarks.

Shared specification, distinct measurements.

Both tracks specify an initial condition, permitted intervention, required change, protected state, and evidence rule. For example, a specification can require moving an object into a particular container while preserving that container’s identity. In an Agent test, the reference environment executes the Agent’s chosen actions and the verifier checks the goal. In a WM test, a prescribed packing action is supplied and generated observations are checked for the requested change and preserved identity. This example explains how the same invariant can be expressed in both tracks; it does not report a matched pair of evaluated episodes. Shared specification principles do not imply shared tasks, numerical scores, or training data.

Diagnostic scope.

The two tracks identify component-level capability gaps under controlled conditions. They do not by themselves establish the cause of a particular coupled failure or whether joint training will yield sustained reciprocal improvement. These questions require matched interaction experiments and evaluation across successive training rounds.

2.3 Agent Examination: Control the World, Test the Agent

The Agent Examination tests whether a candidate MA can complete tasks in a controlled, specification-consistent environment through observation interpretation, state reasoning, planning, action selection, progress verification, and error recovery. Figure 4 summarizes benchmark construction and evaluation.

Benchmark construction. The current Agent inventory contains 1,088 evaluation tasks in 15 reporting categories across four domains: 524 Physical, 255 Digital, 200 Social, and 109 Scientific. The Scientific domain combines 63 selected tasks from Agents’ Last Exam (ALE), 30 scientific code-repair tasks sourced from SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2023), ten ToolChoice tasks derived from the repair workflows, and six EdgeBench optimization tasks (Zhu et al., 2026a). Each ToolChoice task inherits its parent repair task’s subject category but constitutes a distinct evaluated decision checkpoint. The 109 tasks therefore include 99 full workflows and ten checkpoints; their related provenance does not imply independent observations. Six EdgeBench optimization tasks are included; the other 84 historical ALE tasks remain excluded. Table 5 gives the category counts, while Table 10 separates subject category from task source.

Evaluation and aggregation. Task-specific scores are reported on a 0–100 scale. A score can represent strict completion or graded performance according to the corresponding task’s evaluation rule; the values should not all be interpreted as binary success rates. For model configuration mm, category score sm,cs_{m,c}, and category count ncn_{c}, the reported Index is

Im=∑cnc​sm,c1088.I_{m}=\frac{\sum_{c}n_{c}s_{m,c}}{1088}.

Physical, Digital, Social, and Scientific tasks contribute approximately 48.16%, 23.44%, 18.38%, and 10.02%, respectively. These weights describe the selected inventory rather than domain importance. For each Scientific category cc, let ncALEn_{c}^{\mathrm{ALE}} and sm,cALEs_{m,c}^{\mathrm{ALE}} denote its original count and displayed mean, and let bm,j∈{0,1}b_{m,j}\in\{0,1\} be strict success on an added task. We compute

sm,c=ncALE​sm,cALE+100​∑j∈SWEc∪ToolChoicecbm,j+∑j∈Edgecem,jncALE+ncSWE+ncToolChoice+ncEdge.s_{m,c}=\frac{n_{c}^{\mathrm{ALE}}s_{m,c}^{\mathrm{ALE}}+100\sum_{j\in\mathrm{SWE}_{c}\cup\mathrm{ToolChoice}_{c}}b_{m,j}+\sum_{j\in\mathrm{Edge}_{c}}e_{m,j}}{n_{c}^{\mathrm{ALE}}+n_{c}^{\mathrm{SWE}}+n_{c}^{\mathrm{ToolChoice}}+n_{c}^{\mathrm{Edge}}}.

Here em,j∈[0,100]e_{m,j}\in[0,100] is the Edge task score under our aggregation convention. For Borden and DABIC we define e=min⁡(100,max⁡(0,sraw))e=\min(100,\max(0,s_{\mathrm{raw}})); this clipping is introduced by Dual Exam and is not an official EdgeBench normalization rule. Raw values are retained in Appendix A.13. Original ALE and other category means retain their published one-decimal precision; derived Scientific means and Index are computed before final rounding. This preserves the published baseline rather than reconstructing unavailable unrounded means. ToolChoice uses strict full-pass scores, not its auxiliary partial-credit score. Appendix A.2 reports equal-domain weighting, and the Scientific evaluation notes document configuration differences and scoring limitations.

2.4 World Model Examination: Control the Actions, Test the World Model

The World Model Examination fixes action selection and tests whether a candidate WM correctly realizes specification-valid interventions while preserving prior state, identities, and shared-state consistency and obeying active rules. Figure 5 summarizes case construction and evaluation.

Benchmark construction. The World Model evaluation comprises 400 cases across eight scenarios, with 50 cases per scenario: Embodiment, Driving, and Daily Life in the Physical domain; Web and Game in the Digital domain; Human Interaction in the Social domain; and Natural Science and Expert Science in the Scientific domain. Cases specify interventions and checks for requested action effects, preservation of prior state and identities, shared-state consistency, and rule adherence. This allocation gives 150 Physical, 100 Digital, 50 Social, and 100 Scientific cases. Case construction and validation are distinct from independent verification of scores assigned to model outputs.

Evaluation and aggregation. Each rollout uses fixed interventions and the observations and history permitted by its configuration. Case-specific checks assess action effects, state and identity preservation, shared-state consistency, and rule adherence. Observable model errors remain evaluation outcomes; technical failures and unsupported scenarios must be recorded separately. WM Overall is the mean of the eight scenario scores on a 0–100 scale. With 50 cases per scenario, this is also a case-balanced aggregate when each scenario score averages the same number of equally weighted case scores. It is not an equal-domain average: the scenario allocation gives Physical, Digital, Social, and Scientific weights of 37.5%, 25%, 12.5%, and 25%. Missing scenario scores are not zeros. A mean over fewer scenarios must be labeled as partial coverage and must not enter the full-coverage Overall ranking.

Modality and execution scope.

Table 4 separates image and video configurations. The shared target is observable task-consistent state evolution; video additionally supplies temporal evidence unavailable from a static checkpoint. A plausible still image cannot establish timing or an oscillation period. Text-only World Models are outside this visual-observation scope and would require a separately specified observation interface and rubric. Per-configuration histories, duration, budgets, and missing provenance limit cross-modality interpretation (Appendix C).

3 Experiments

Following the coupled pilot, we evaluate the two components separately. Table 3 compares 10 Agent configurations across 15 reporting categories and 1,088 evaluation items. The World Model evaluation uses 400 cases across eight scenarios, with 50 cases per scenario; Table 4 reports scenario scores and distinguishes full from partial coverage. Agent Index and WM Overall use different tasks, metrics, and aggregation rules and are not directly comparable. Appendices A and B provide illustrative trajectories. These examples explain particular behaviors rather than estimate failure frequencies or establish controlled comparisons between historical configurations.

3.1 Agent Results: RQ1

Execution performance varies across task settings.

The fixed-environment track measures Agent performance without variation from a candidate World Model. The highest displayed scores are 9.5 for Manipulation, 11.2 for Action Sequencing, and 5.6 for Desktop Application Interaction. Other settings yield higher maxima: 29.6 for Web Interaction, 42.9 for Mobile Application Interaction, and 47.1 for Game Environment Interaction. These contrasts describe performance under the respective task requirements and scoring rules; they do not isolate the effect of the interaction setting or establish equal difficulty across categories. The results nevertheless show that a high aggregate score can coexist with low scores on particular execution tasks.

Locally correct elements may fail to form a valid solution.

The illustrative Navigation cases distinguish valid feasibility judgments from routes containing nonexistent edges. The Action Sequencing cases similarly distinguish correct clip membership from correct ordering. In each setting, recognizing relevant elements is insufficient when their combination violates the task’s constraints. These examples motivate explicit checks of route validity, ordering, and goal satisfaction during execution. They illustrate possible failure mechanisms but do not establish their frequency in the current evaluation or their causal contribution to model rankings.

Scientific scores combine distinct evaluation units.

Across 109 Scientific items, GPT 6 Astra has the highest within-domain case-weighted score of 50.6, followed by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at 44.0 and GPT 5.6 Sol at 42.2. The category leaders differ: Astra leads Mathematics & Computation (60.8) and Physical Sciences (52.2), Sol leads Health & Medicine (45.4), and DeepSeek leads Life Sciences (53.7). These scores combine 63 ALE tasks, 30 SWE-bench repair tasks, ten derived ToolChoice checkpoints, and six EdgeBench optimization tasks. SWE and ToolChoice contribute strict binary outcomes, while Edge contributes graded quality scores under the mapping in Appendix A.13, including our explicit clipping convention for Borden and DABIC. The domain mean is therefore not a uniform success rate, and the related ToolChoice checkpoints do not constitute independent full-workflow trials.

Aggregate rank depends on task composition.

GPT 6 Astra leads the case-weighted Agent Index with 31.3, followed by GPT 5.6 Sol at 20.7 and Gemini 3.6 Flash at 20.1. Qwen 3.8 Max ranks fourth at 20.0 and Kimi K3 fifth at 19.8. Four configurations attain the highest displayed score in at least one category: GPT 6 Astra leads nine categories, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash leads three, GPT 5.6 Sol leads two, and Seed 2.1 Pro leads one. No configuration leads every category. Equal-domain weighting changes several positions: DeepSeek moves from sixth to second and Kimi from fifth to fourth, while GPT 6 Astra remains first (Appendix A.2). Physical tasks account for 48.16% of Index and Scientific tasks for 10.02%; these weights reflect the inventory rather than equal domain importance. These rankings describe the chosen aggregation rules and evaluated model–harness configurations. Small differences derived from rounded baseline means do not establish statistically significant superiority.

3.2 World Model Results: RQ2

Action responsiveness must preserve accumulated progress.

The fixed-intervention track tests whether valid action inputs produce valid state evolution. Its illustrative failures show that responding to the current instruction is only part of this requirement. Qwen-Image-3.0 restores the apparatus view following an instruction in the pendulum case (Appendix Figure 21), but introduces additional cups in the cup-stacking case, violating the initial quantity constraint (Appendix Figure 23). MiniMax H3 preserves the cup count yet introduces an unrequested red tray, whereas GPT-Image-2 preserves the original tray colors (Appendix Figure 24). These cases illustrate distinct failures in realizing requested changes and preserving unaffected state; they do not establish the causes of aggregate ranking differences. In coupled interaction, such state errors can become misleading observations for the Agent.

Digital scenarios remain challenging across configurations.

All evaluated configurations score at most 16.5 on Web and 13.3 on Game (Table 4). Even models with stronger results elsewhere remain weak in these scenarios: MiniMax H3 scores 53.8 on Embodiment but only 3.7 on Web and 8.5 on Game, while Qwen-Image-3.0 scores 46.1 on Daily Life but 10.7 on Web and 11.5 on Game. These results identify digital scenarios as a shared weakness under the evaluated protocol, although differences in task difficulty and scoring prevent attributing the gap solely to the domain.

Scenario averages do not establish suitability for a partner Agent.

GPT-Image-2 leads WM Overall with 21.7 versus 17.3 for MiniMax H3, but their ordering reverses on Embodiment, at 20.9 versus 53.8. WM Overall weights the eight scenarios equally, whereas a particular Agent may encounter a different distribution of states and actions. A higher overall score therefore need not imply more reliable responses along that Agent’s trajectories. Scenario profiles narrow this uncertainty, but selecting an effective Agent–World Model pairing requires evaluation on the interactions the pair actually produces.

Joint perspective.

Reliable task progress requires both effective Agent decisions and World Model responses that correctly realize action effects while preserving task-relevant state, since these responses also inform the Agent’s judgment of progress. The two tracks assess these complementary capabilities, but do not establish how their scores jointly predict coupled success.

4 Discussion

4.1 Related Work

Existing benchmarks typically assess one component. Agent benchmarks measure tool use, collaboration, workplace execution, transferable skills, and long-horizon computer operation (Liu et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024; Barres et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026), whereas World Model benchmarks evaluate prediction, embodied functionality, latent dynamics, memory, action control, and behavioral consistency (Shang et al., 2026b; Chen et al., 2025; Vafa et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026). These benchmarks assess competence, not reciprocal improvement.

Prior work supports both directions. Dyna and learned World Models use simulated trajectories to improve planning and policies (Sutton, 1990; Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026). Conversely, Agent-directed exploration and policy rollouts improve held-out World Model learning or adapt simulators (Kim et al., 2020; Chebotar et al., 2019), while recent methods refine World Models from interaction feedback (Zhang et al., 2026b; Yu et al., 2026). DreamZero jointly predicts video and actions for robot control and reports transfer to new tasks and embodiments (Ye et al., 2026a). Such results support studying action-conditioned visual models in embodied systems; they do not validate our cross-domain rankings or establish a reciprocal training loop. These gains are demonstrated within bounded task distributions. Narrow-domain systems begin to close the loop. WebEvolver (Fang et al., 2025) couples Agent experience with an evolving World Model, GenEnv co-evolves LLM Agents and environment simulators, and COMAP alternates World Model and policy updates (Fang et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026).

4.2 Toward Agent–World Model Co-evolution

World Models can improve Agents through simulated experience, as DreamerV3 demonstrates across diverse control tasks (Hafner et al., 2025). Such benefits depend on controlling model bias: MBPO uses short simulated rollouts to support policy learning (Janner et al., 2019). The relevant test is whether this experience improves Agent behavior beyond the model used for training.

Agents can, in turn, improve World Models by collecting informative interaction data. Directed exploration improves predictive model learning (Kim et al., 2020), while SimOpt uses real policy rollouts to refine simulator parameter distributions and improve policy transfer (Chebotar et al., 2019). These updates improve the model or simulator; the Agent’s task score alone does not measure the collected data’s training value.

Connecting these directions offers a route to co-evolution, but separate gains do not establish a stable loop. WebEvolver links them by training a World Model on Agent trajectories and using it for policy training and look-ahead planning (Fang et al., 2025). We hypothesize that reciprocal improvement across broader multimodal tasks may become sustainable once both components reach sufficient task-specific competence, but neither this transition nor the required capability levels has been established.

Dual Exam diagnoses component capabilities rather than co-evolution itself. Our observed execution and state-consistency failures identify possible obstacles to useful interaction, not evidence of limited learnability. In the packing case, commands continue after the container changes (Figure 2); this observation motivates diagnosis but does not test whether either component can learn from the interaction. Future work should compare joint updates with Agent-only, World-Model-only, and no-update controls, using fixed held-out tests across rounds and seeds to track both components and closed-loop task success. This would test whether both components improve over successive rounds and whether these gains translate into more reliable joint task performance.

Implications for system design.

The observed cases suggest concrete targets for subsequent experiments. Invalid routes and action orders motivate explicit checks of global constraints before committing to a sequence. Changes in container identity, object count, or unrelated scene attributes motivate verification that requested updates preserve protected state. Resource-allocation examples motivate checks of joint constraints rather than individual choices alone. These are hypotheses motivated by illustrative failures, not established explanations of aggregate performance. Their utility should be tested through controlled interventions on the same cases, measuring both strict task completion and any separately defined intermediate progress.

4.3 Evaluation Limitations

Evaluation limitations.

The reported scores depend on task selection, reference environments, verification rules, and configuration-specific execution settings. Fixed conditions reduce one source of variation but do not establish that the reference mechanism is error-free. The current presentation does not report an independent, stratified agreement estimate for the World Model output scores. The packing audit is additionally retrospective: its rubric was specified after inspecting the trajectory, and its labels have not been independently adjudicated. These limits should be addressed by documenting environment validation, auditing scored outputs independently, and reporting disagreements, ambiguous checks, and invalid-run counts. Such evidence is needed to quantify measurement reliability beyond the illustrative examples.

Scientific aggregation and evidence coverage.

The Scientific scores combine binary repair and checkpoint outcomes with graded optimization results. Our clipping of Borden and DABIC to [0,100][0,100] is a Dual Exam aggregation convention, not an official EdgeBench normalization rule; a shared range does not equate task difficulty. We retain valid Edge submissions recorded within the selected run’s allowance of at most 43,200 seconds, including submissions before early termination. This does not imply that every run completed the full horizon. The supplied trace archive is truncated: the four added configurations’ Wireless endpoints were checked against their best-submission judge reports, but the remaining added-task endpoints and evaluator-version equivalence have not all been independently verified. Execution harnesses also differ across configurations. Appendix A.13 preserves raw objectives and details these evidence limits.

Limits of the comparisons.

The leaderboard reports descriptive point scores, without repeated-run uncertainty estimates or significance tests. Differences between configurations therefore do not establish statistically significant superiority. Original category means are available only to one decimal place, so derived aggregates retain this baseline precision limit. The separate tracks also do not establish how component scores predict coupled performance. Action-sensitive validation would benefit from controls such as unchanged-frame, no-op, and shuffled-intervention outputs, with scoring targets defined in advance for each control. Matched interaction experiments and repeated evaluations are needed to test robustness, partner suitability, and the effect of corrective feedback. These questions are distinct from the descriptive rankings reported here.

Unperformed controls and next tests.

We have not run copy-last-frame, no-op, or shuffled-action baselines for the present WM scores. A copy-last-frame control should be scored against the original requested changes and protected-state checks separately; a true no-op intervention should instead use an identity-transition target, and shuffled interventions require targets derived from the shuffled sequence. These controls test different failure modes and should not share an incompatible target. Likewise, budget curves and correction-versus-repetition tests require matched cases and equal resources. Existing multi-attempt illustrations are descriptive and do not substitute for such controls. A stratified independent output audit remains necessary before claiming calibrated judge reliability.

5 Conclusion

Dual Exam evaluates Multimodal Agents under fixed environment response mechanisms and World Models under fixed action interventions, producing complementary performance profiles across four domains. The Agent evaluation compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories; GPT 6 Astra achieves the highest case-weighted Index of 31.3. The World Model evaluation contains 400 cases across eight scenarios, with 50 cases per scenario. GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall scores at 21.7. Configuration-specific coverage is reported separately, and the two tracks use different tasks and metrics, so their aggregate scores are not directly comparable. Scientific evaluation spans 109 items and combines strict repair and checkpoint outcomes with graded optimization scores; Astra leads its within-domain aggregate at 50.6. Category leaders differ, and equal-domain weighting changes the overall ordering below the leading configuration. The results characterize model–harness performance under the evaluated specifications and weighting choices, subject to the documented evidence and precision limits. Predicting coupled success and demonstrating sustained reciprocal improvement require matched interaction and learning experiments beyond these separate assessments.

Appendix A Details of Agent Evaluation

This appendix describes the Agent evaluation across four domains and distinguishes the current reporting inventory from historical illustrative cases. The current leaderboard contains 1,088 items in 15 categories: four Physical, four Digital, three Social, and four Scientific categories. Appendix A.1 defines their scope and counts.

The figures include reference demonstrations, execution screenshots, saved predictions, and recorded outcomes. Reference demonstrations illustrate intended behavior; model trajectories illustrate particular successes or failures. Historical workflow-oriented headings are not additional categories in the current leaderboard, and illustrative cases do not by themselves establish coverage or model rankings. Historical examples are used here to explain task requirements and scoring behavior, rather than to support quantitative conclusions about the current inventory.

A.1 Domain Selection, Task Categories, and Interpretation

Purpose of the classification.

We organize the agent evaluation using three levels: domains, task categories, and individual evaluation items. The four domains provide complementary settings for examining goal-directed behavior: Physical concerns actions and constraints in physical scenes; Digital concerns interaction with software interfaces; Social concerns decisions involving other agents and shared resources; and Scientific concerns technical workflows with checkable scientific or computational deliverables. This is an operational organization of the selected benchmark tasks, rather than an exhaustive taxonomy of intelligence or evidence that the domains measure independent latent abilities. In particular, scientific tasks can use digital interfaces, and physical tasks can involve both planning and manipulation.

Category granularity.

Within each domain, categories describe the distinctions supported by its task collection. Physical categories emphasize task demands, Digital categories emphasize interaction environments, Social categories distinguish strategic interaction and resource-governance settings, and Scientific categories organize subject matter. We therefore use task categories, rather than treating all category labels as equivalent, mutually exclusive cognitive capabilities. The mixed organizing criteria support interpretable reporting of this inventory but limit claims about universal capability coverage.

Physical: planning versus sequence reconstruction.

The recorded task descriptions provide a concrete distinction. Planning involves organizing dependent actions to satisfy household goals, illustrated by dinner preparation and household restoration. Action Sequencing instead presents initial and target states together with a shuffled pool of action clips: each problem requires assigning clips to two tasks and reconstructing both reference orders. This distinction is between goal-directed planning and constrained sequence reconstruction, not between the presence and absence of planning ability. Navigation evaluates agent-specific traversability and valid routes, whereas Manipulation evaluates changes to object configurations. Success in one category should not be interpreted as isolating a single cognitive mechanism.

Digital: environments rather than independent faculties.

The four categories identify the primary interaction setting. Web Interaction covers browser-based tasks; desktop and mobile categories identify application environments; game tasks are reported separately as game environments. These settings share requirements such as perception, planning, interface operation, and recovery from errors. A game accessed through a browser can consequently overlap conceptually with web interaction. For reproducible aggregation, each item retains one primary reporting assignment in the inventory; shared demands can be described separately without counting the item twice. The platform label alone does not establish a distinct underlying capability.

Social: three task families and their limits.

The 200 social cases instantiate 40 task templates. Coordination & Strategic Interaction contains 87 cases from 17 templates, including bargaining, congestion coordination, public-goods dilemmas, negotiation, and persuasion. The remaining two families both involve shared-resource decisions: 56 cases from 11 templates concern aquatic, soil, and climate resources, while 57 cases from 12 templates concern terrestrial ecosystems, agricultural or forest resources, and health-related resources such as antibiotics. We retain these two settings for separate reporting because they specify different resource contexts; this is not evidence that they measure two independent governance abilities. Ecological boundaries can overlap, so the task’s recorded primary resource setting determines its reporting assignment. The older labels Natural Allocation and Society Access are replaced here by descriptions of the actual task content.

Scientific: subject areas and cross-disciplinary cases.

The current scientific inventory contains 109 tasks: 63 ALE tasks, 30 SWE-bench repair tasks, ten derived ToolChoice tasks, and six EdgeBench optimization tasks. Its subject labels are reporting assignments, not an assertion that scientific disciplines have disjoint methods. Health & Medicine emphasizes health-related objectives, whereas Life Sciences emphasizes biological investigation; Mathematics & Computation includes tasks organized around mathematical or computational outputs. Existing assignments are retained for score traceability, including cross-disciplinary cases: for example, the quantum Ising-chain computation is assigned to Mathematics & Computation in the source mapping. A stricter subject-based reassignment would require an explicit revision and recomputation of category scores.

The original 13-item ALE Physical Sciences group includes materials and molecular calculations, but also climate simulation, lake-model calibration, orbital transfer, and Hubble-image processing. Consequently, neither Materials Science nor Physics & Chemistry fully describes this set. Here Physical Sciences denotes a scientific subject group spanning physics, chemistry, and Earth and space applications; Physical denotes the separate action-oriented domain. A more explicit display label is Physics, Chemistry, Earth & Space Sciences. Changing the display label does not move tasks between categories. The group also contains a stochastic chemical-kinetics task involving a gene-regulatory network, illustrating the limits of a single primary assignment.

Inventory scope and counting units.

The current Agent inventory contains 1,088 evaluation tasks in 15 reporting categories across four domains: 524 Physical, 255 Digital, 200 Social, and 109 Scientific. The Scientific domain combines 63 selected tasks from Agents’ Last Exam (ALE), 30 scientific code-repair tasks sourced from SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2023), ten ToolChoice tasks derived from the repair workflows, and six EdgeBench optimization tasks. Each ToolChoice task inherits its parent repair task’s subject category but constitutes a distinct evaluated decision checkpoint. The 109 tasks therefore include 99 full workflows and ten checkpoints; their related provenance does not imply independent observations. Six EdgeBench optimization tasks are included; the other 84 historical ALE tasks remain excluded. Table 5 gives the category counts, while Table 10 separates subject category from task source.

A.2 Sensitivity to Domain Weighting

The reported Index weights task categories by their configured item counts. To examine dependence on the domain mixture, we additionally average the four within-domain case-weighted scores:

Imequal​-​domain=14​∑d∑c∈dnc​sm,c∑c∈dnc.I_{m}^{\mathrm{equal\mbox{-}domain}}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{d}\frac{\sum_{c\in d}n_{c}s_{m,c}}{\sum_{c\in d}n_{c}}.

Both calculations retain the original one-decimal category means as baseline and incorporate the added binary outcomes and graded Edge scores before final rounding. The extra decimal shown here explains the computed ordering but does not recover lost baseline precision. This is an aggregation sensitivity analysis, not an uncertainty estimate.

GPT 6 Astra ranks first under both mixtures, but several other positions change substantially. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash moves from sixth to second and Kimi K3 from fifth to fourth. The case-weighted Index should therefore be interpreted as performance on the configured inventory rather than a distribution-independent ordering of general Agent ability. Confidence intervals and paired model comparisons require the underlying evaluation records and a resampling unit that accounts for shared templates and the SWE/ToolChoice parent links. In particular, the 200 Social cases instantiate 40 templates and should not automatically be treated as independent observations.

Figure 6 introduces four task workflows through reference demonstrations D1–D4, pairing a scene image with selected actions and the final goal indicators. These are demonstrations of the required behavior, rather than evaluated model predictions. Figure 7 presents two successful and two unsuccessful episodes, using head-camera frames from the start, midpoint, and near the end. Each episode uses seed 0. Official results supply the success flag and the score on a 0–1 scale; the sampled frames describe the attempt without identifying its exact failure mechanism.

The physical model evaluations use reasoning effort high and each model’s maximum supported output-token limit. These settings do not apply to the planning reference demonstrations. The manipulation recordings also use different historical controller configurations, so they support case interpretation rather than a controlled model comparison. The stored InternVLA_A15 / arx_x5 label identifies the setup without separately verifying the upstream planning model.

A.5 Navigation

Navigation tests whether an Agent can infer who can traverse a scene and produce a valid route. Each of the 282 questions supplies a scene-tour video and asks for decisions for five agent types: HUMAN, WHEELCHAIR, HUMANOID, QUADRUPEDAL, and SWEEPER. A question passes only if all five feasibility decisions are correct and every required route connects the specified endpoints through existing, traversable graph edges. Figure 8 separates these two checks by showing feasibility decisions alongside the predicted HUMAN route.

The four cases use saved Gemini 3.6 Flash predictions and include two successes and two failures. We checked the predictions against the specified task maps and movement rules. Scene images identify the environment rather than the precise route endpoints, and the displayed reference is one valid route rather than the only permitted answer. The saved predictions are checked against the available task definitions; later responses and reindexed copies are excluded because the original API responses are unavailable.

  • •

    N1: Valid routes for two agent types. In scene HM3D00000 (question 00000011), the route runs from the living-room fireplace area to the master-bedroom wardrobe. The model correctly permits HUMAN and QUADRUPEDAL and rejects the other three types. Both required routes are valid, so all five outputs pass the combined feasibility and route checks.

  • •

    N2: Valid routes for three agent types. In scene HM3D00027 (question 00000871), the route runs from a living-room sofa to the kitchen stove. HUMAN, QUADRUPEDAL, and SWEEPER are feasible, and the evaluated model supplies valid routes for them. All five outputs pass; accessibility depends on the specific scene and destination.

  • •

    N3: Correct feasibility, invalid routes. In scene HM3D00002 (question 00000051), all five feasibility decisions are correct, but the HUMAN and QUADRUPEDAL routes include the nonexistent edge from node 6 to node 7. The accompanying figure shows this missing connection in red. Only three of five complete outputs pass, because correctly predicting that a destination is reachable does not guarantee that the proposed route reaches it.

  • •

    N4: Incorrect feasibility and routes. In scene MP3D00003 (question 00001471), the reference permits only HUMAN, whereas the evaluated model permits all five types. The model-predicted routes also contain the nonexistent edge from node 45 to node 40. Thus, one feasibility decision is correct but no complete output passes; the case illustrates separate errors in assessing accessibility and constructing a route through the scene.

A.6 Action Sequencing

Action Sequencing assesses whether an Agent can reconstruct actions that connect an initial state to a target state. Each of the 170 problems contains two tasks and one shared, shuffled pool of action clips. The evaluated model must assign every clip to a task and order the resulting sequences without being told their lengths. Success requires an exact match to both reference sequences. Figures 9–12 place the initial and target states above the clip pool and compare the reference and model-predicted orders for each task for direct comparison.

The examples use saved Qwen3.8-max-preview predictions, checked against the fixed task definitions, with two successes and two failures. Clip IDs retain their original meaning within each problem. Blue tokens denote the reference; green and red prediction tokens mark agreement or disagreement at the same sequence position. Original API responses are not available, and later generated responses and reindexed copies are excluded from the analysis.

  • •

    W1: Correct sequences of different lengths. CrossTask pair 013 combines food preparation and a wheel-change task. The predicted sequences [7, 2, 6] and [5, 1, 4, 3] match both references, correctly dividing seven clips into groups of three and four. Figure 9 depicts exact reconstruction of both sequences without assuming equal lengths.

  • •

The model predicts [3, 5, 4, 1] and [7, 6, 2, 8], matching both four-step references. Figure 10 shows that all eight clips are assigned and ordered correctly despite the visual similarity of the two preparation and application workflows.

  • •

    W3: Correct clips in the wrong order. COIN pair 002 combines a filter-replacement task with work on a bicycle. The references are [5, 3, 2] and [6, 4, 1], but the evaluated model predicts [3, 5, 2] and [4, 1, 6]. Each task receives the correct clips, yet neither order matches. The positional mismatches in Figure 11 demonstrate that identifying the relevant clips and ordering them correctly are separate requirements for task success in the required workflow.

The evaluated model instead returns [9, 6, 10, 4, 1] and [8, 2, 3, 7, 5]. Figure 12 depicts a five-plus-five division rather than the required four-plus-six division. The numerical tables below use these abbreviations. These tasks assess whether an Agent can use interface observations and tool feedback to complete a concrete request. Evidence and scope.

The browsing cases show five improvements and five contrasting failures across repeated attempts; none earns full credit. The desktop, mobile, and game-control cases meet their respective task criteria. A separate kitchen-planning demonstration and ten reference scene views explain interactive planning tasks. These sources have different purposes and are not combined into a single success rate; changes across browsing attempts also do not isolate the effect of memory from differences in tool activity or evaluation conditions.

A.7 Web Interaction

Web browsing assesses whether an Agent can turn product requirements into purchasing information supported by identifiable sources. Each task requires finding suitable configurations, checking all requested properties, collecting exact purchase pages with displayed prices, and submitting a report. The evaluation distinguishes a filled answer field from a verified claim, so broad product coverage alone is insufficient for a high score and a fully supported report.

The eight selected cases cover seven tasks and five model labels. I1–I5 illustrate increasing verification credit, while F1–F3 illustrate declining scores, unsupported coverage, incomplete answers, or no score improvement. Each case has three attempts, denoted R1–R3. The largest displayed score is 27.50%, so an improvement remains partial instead of indicating completion of the task. The I labels retain source cases S1–S5 and mark improvement rather than success.

Each task requests 30 product/configuration entries and three purchase pages per entry. One compound attribute item is scored per entry, plus one item per purchase page:

Verified score=attribute credits (out of 30)+page credits (out of 90)120.\text{Verified score}=\frac{\text{attribute credits (out of 30)}+\text{page credits (out of 90)}}{120}.

Submission coverage and local evidence-save acceptance are separate diagnostics. A credited page does not establish that its product satisfies every hardware constraint.

Interpreting browsing outcomes.

The analysis uses saved execution records, submitted answers, and evaluator results. It describes the recorded product evidence rather than current prices or availability. Different tool activity and the lack of a matched control without memory prevent causal or efficiency comparisons across attempts. Accepted quotations and final evaluation credits are distinct, and zero credit does not prove every claim false.

Descriptions of memory follow the actual inputs in each execution record. Separate memory files disagree with those inputs in six R2/R3 comparisons involving I1, I3, and I4, so they are not substituted for the recorded context. We also distinguish the original submissions from later answer files containing additional evidence. Some tool returns were shortened before archiving; their omitted content is unavailable for further verification.

  • •

    I1: Telescope selection with stronger supporting evidence. Qwen 3.8 Max is asked to find 30 complete telescope configurations with an aperture of at least eight inches, a computerized GoTo mount, and an included tripod or ground-standing base. Each configuration needs three exact purchasing pages with displayed prices; search and category pages do not qualify. The execution instructions require source inspection and saved quotations before factual claims are included in the report submitted through submit_answer.

R1 receives the original request, while R2 and R3 also receive recorded memory and task state. The three attempts contain 322 messages and 223 tool calls in total. Each has 31 model calls, but the amount of tool activity differs, as shown below. The table separates accepted evidence saves from the attribute and purchase-page credits awarded to the final answer.

Save counts describe accepted quotations; attribute and page counts describe the final evaluation. The three rounds each contain 31 Agent model calls, with distinct amounts of retrieval and other tool activity.

In R1, the evaluated Agent retrieves a NexStar 8SE product record containing a price of $1,699 and saves the quotation successfully. However, the price alone does not establish the required aperture, mount, and included support. After 54 JSON requests, seven page opens, and three searches, the Agent submits only a research-in-progress placeholder. No credit is awarded because the useful price evidence never becomes a usable final answer.

In R2, the Agent uses smaller retrieval batches and individual product records to recover usable prices. The final answer includes two configurations: NexStar 8SE, with Celestron and Astronomics pages priced at $1,699, and Advanced VX 11 SCT, with a Celestron page priced at $3,599. These are three pages in total, rather than three per configuration. Two attribute and three page credits yield 4.17%, leaving most of the requested report incomplete.

In R3, retrieval becomes more specific to each configuration. The evaluated Agent saves product prices and some tripod descriptions, and excludes candidates without preserved prices or with insufficient aperture. The final answer contains 16 configurations and 17 credited purchase pages, producing (16+17)/120=27.50%(16+17)/120=27.50\%. NexStar 8SE has two pages and each remaining entry has one; no configuration meets the three-page requirement. Tripod evidence is explicit for only five configurations, so the archived attribute credits should not be interpreted as independent verification of every hardware condition.

The telescope case therefore progresses from an unusable submission to a small supported answer and then to a broader, still incomplete report. The increase concerns evidence preserveed in the answer, rather than the number of searches alone. It illustrates the practical distinction among discovering candidates, documenting their properties, and delivering all requested information, while leaving the contribution of memory unresolved.

Capability interpretation.

The cases separate candidate discovery, submission coverage, evidence capture, and verified correctness. Progress occurs when retrieval is converted into specific supporting evidence in a report that the evaluator can assess. Failure persists when broad coverage masks missing purchase evidence, quotations do not support compound constraints, or the final answer remains incomplete. The telescope case illustrates a clearer path from retrieval to documented evidence, while its missing configurations and purchase pages explain why the higher score remains partial instead of complete.

Desktop tasks evaluate visual inspection, application operation, and file editing against task-specific deliverable checks. The current leaderboard contains 95 tasks in this category.
