Planning across interactive scenes.

The following ten interactive tasks exercise planning and environment interaction across five simulated scene families: an office, an apartment, a garden, a restaurant, and a staircase. Figure 14 summarizes their environments and objectives. We then examine a complete conveyor-kitchen demonstration, pairing every action batch with its returned observation and terminal outcome. All interfaces are in English. The kitchen run is a non-blind illustration, separate from the recorded benchmark evaluations.

  • •

    G2: Deadline-aware planning in a conveyor kitchen.

    The agent operates a conveyor-belt kitchen for ten one-minute windows. It observes 16 ingredient plates, a fixed recipe menu, current demand multipliers, and market forecasts, then selects ingredients and serves dishes to maximize net profit. Each window allows one dish; each recipe can be served at most twice. Ingredient selections are irreversible, recipes require exactly the listed ingredients, and invalid dishes incur ingredient costs and lock the window. Demand changes selling prices while ingredient costs remain fixed. Under this exact-ingredient rule, extra ingredients are a violation even if the dish looks plausible; the criterion is not relaxed after observing a rollout. A successful dish or a positive profit is intermediate evidence, not by itself satisfaction of the final profit threshold and all constraints.

This run requires two salads by window 3 (+$8 reward / -$10 penalty), one sandwich by window 6 (+$10 / -$12), and at least four dish categories by window 10 (+$12 / -$15). Rewards or penalties settle at the respective deadlines. Success requires net profit, after these adjustments, to reach 90% of the hidden online benchmark before the 150-call limit.

C denotes a tool-call index and O an observation ID. The notation select [a,b,c] denotes ordered ingredient selections within one action batch. C01 requests the briefing, C02 obtains the starting observation, C03–C32 execute 30 action batches, and C33 stops the session. Figures 15–17 contain all 30 recorded observations O01–O30: the initial observation and 29 images returned after action batches. C32 supplies the terminal event without producing another image. The sequence consequently ends with observation O30, while the adjacent annotation records the outcome returned by the final action batch in this run.

Figures 15–17 show how early deadlines shape later choices. A burger in window 1 is followed by two salads, meeting the first contract by window 3. Soups occupy windows 4 and 5, and a sandwich meets the second deadline in window 6. The remaining windows contain an omelet, two sandwiches, and another omelet. Each row links the current window, selected ingredients, and accepted dish, while the annotations separate dish profit from contract payments.

The terminal event reports success with reason efficiency_target_reached. It returns no new screenshot, exact efficiency percentage, or post-settlement balance; $230 is the last observed pre-settlement balance. The demonstration exercises ten-window planning, recipe-limit tracking, and deadline-aware contract completion. Prior exposure and an interrupted attempt make this a non-blind demonstration instead of a new benchmark evaluation.

A.11 Digital World: Historical Cross-Attempt Results

Table 8 retains the six configurations in the historical multi-attempt snapshot that belong to the current leaderboard. These historical means use all accepted records within each configuration and attempt; coverage can vary, so they are not replacements for the current leaderboard scores. Kimi K3 has no accepted Mobile Application Interaction results in attempts 2 and 3. We report model-specific means only; pooled statistics and fixed-cohort curves from the previous model set are not used for the revised inventory. These are descriptive trajectories, not controlled estimates of the effect of repetition or reflection.

Social evaluation inventory and example scope.

The Social evaluation comprises 200 cases in three reporting categories: Coordination & Strategic Interaction (87), Water, Soil & Climate Resource Governance (56), and Terrestrial Ecosystem & Health Resource Governance (57). The cases instantiate 40 templates (17, 11, and 12, respectively); Appendix A.1 explains these assignments. Task counts are unaffected by the number of model runs or attempt stages.

The resource examples below illustrate the two resource-governance categories; they are selected historical traces, not representative coverage of all social templates.

A.12 Resource-Governance Examples: Groundwater and Forests

Reporting categories versus execution mechanisms.

The resource inventory contains 56 Water, Soil & Climate Resource Governance cases and 57 Terrestrial Ecosystem & Health Resource Governance cases. Inspecting the available trajectories distinguishes two mechanisms within these scene-based categories: the first contains 20 resource-extraction cases and 36 capacity-allocation cases; the second contains six resource-extraction cases and 51 capacity-allocation cases. Thus 87 of the 113 resource-labelled cases execute a capacity-allocation game, while 26 execute a resource-extraction game. These are case counts by observed mechanism, not performance measurements or claims of independent governance abilities. For example, an antibiotics-labelled allocation trace asks twelve participants to choose among four channels of capacity three; it does not simulate antimicrobial resistance. The two examples below use the resource-extraction mechanism and illustrate one scene from each reporting category.

Source and shared rules.

Both records retain the source model identifier anthropic/claude-fable-5; we do not infer equivalence to another leaderboard configuration. The groundwater record is task card social.commons.aquifer.v0, strict100 case suffix 018d88e51fdb6e3d; the forest record is task card social.commons.forest.v0, archive case1. Each provides 72 prompt–response entries and a six-round state log. These selected historical failure traces explain the task mechanism and do not estimate a failure rate or establish a model ranking.

In each simplified game, twelve independently queried operators choose their own extraction, with no communication or visibility into other operators’ choices. The initial stock is 100 units; the prompt specifies regeneration of the remaining stock, approximately doubling up to a cap of 100, and a sustainable total extraction of 50 units per round. A separate industrial operator always requests 46 units per round, leaving a sustainable allowance of four units for the twelve participants together (one third of a unit each under equal sharing). Participants are instructed to maximize their own cumulative income over six rounds. These are stylized resource games, not validated hydrological or ecological simulators.

Groundwater depletion (Water, Soil & Climate).

The scene is an almond-orchard operator sharing a groundwater basin, with quantities measured in megaliters. The first-round responses, in operator order, are

(10,25,8,8,10,4,4,15,18,4,15,8),(10,25,8,8,10,4,4,15,18,4,15,8),

which sum to 129 requested units before the industrial operator’s request. The state log records a pool of zero after round one and zero participant extraction for rounds two through six. The record reports survived=false, constraint_ok=false, and a raw score of 0.05. The requests exceed available stock and must not be read as 129 units of physically realized extraction.

Forest depletion (Terrestrial Ecosystem & Health).

The second scene is clear-cutting a shared rainforest reserve, with quantities measured in hectares. Its first-round requests are

(20,8,10,10,30,8,10,20,8,10,15,8),(20,8,10,10,30,8,10,20,8,10,15,8),

which sum to 157 units before the industrial request. This record also reaches zero stock after round one and records zero participant extraction in rounds two through six, with survived=false, constraint_ok=false, and raw score 0.05. The shared mechanism permits a direct description of the two trajectories, but their common failure does not establish broad ecological competence or incompetence.

Scientific evaluation context.

The Scientific domain contains 109 evaluation tasks: 63 selected ALE tasks, 30 scientific code-repair tasks sourced from SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2023), ten ToolChoice tasks constructed from those repair workflows, and six EdgeBench optimization tasks. The SWE source collection used here is identified in the local materials as swe-public-30; the ten ToolChoice checkpoints are derived tasks, not an official SWE-bench split. Mathematics & Computation contains 15 tasks, Health & Medicine 25, Life Sciences 32, and Physical Sciences 37. Existing ALE assignments are retained; new repair tasks are assigned by their scientific objective, and ToolChoice inherits its parent task’s category. Physical Sciences includes physics, chemistry, materials, and Earth/space applications and differs from the action-oriented Physical domain.

All 109 tasks enter the Scientific category scores and the 1,088-task Agent Index. There are 99 full workflows and ten decision checkpoints, which need not be statistically independent of their parent workflows. The six EdgeBench optimization tasks are included; the other 84 historical ALE tasks remain excluded.

Added-task scores and evaluation settings.

SWE tasks use the recorded binary verifier reward; ToolChoice tasks use strict full-pass outcomes requiring the prescribed tool, arguments, and call constraints. Each added task receives 100 on success and 0 otherwise. We retain the audited final records, including valid timeout outcomes, rather than selecting the best across alternate harnesses. The retained six configurations use the archived Claude Code SWE runs and ToolChoice records. The four added configurations use the supplied audit of GLM 5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, MiMo V2.5, and GPT 6 Astra. Astra uses a native Codex configuration, whereas the other three use API-based execution. Context, tools, and execution budgets are not fully matched. Seed 2.1 Pro’s 0/30 SWE result primarily reflects failure to enter the Claude Code/API tool loop. Thus these are configuration-level observations, not controlled measurements of model-only ability.

The four-model audit also identifies a ToolChoice specification limitation: six checkpoints (v01, v03, v05, v06, v08, v10) require a task_id argument that is not supplied in the prompt. The archived strict scores are retained without retrospective rescoring; failures on these checkpoints cannot be attributed solely to tool-selection ability. The task manifest’s title for task_001 differs from the current instruction, although both map to Physical Sciences; task IDs and audited outcomes, rather than the ambiguous title, determine this aggregation. Exact upstream SWE-bench instance IDs and revision links remain necessary to establish complete instance-level provenance.

A.13 Edge Task Aggregation and Raw Scores

We include six tasks from EdgeBench (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05155). Wireless Electricity Layout, BipedalWalker Locomotion RL, and Graph Node Classification are assigned to Mathematics & Computation; Borden Source Inversion, Molecular Self Assembly, and DABIC Gravity Inversion are assigned to Physical Sciences. These primary reporting assignments do not establish disciplinary exclusivity.

Dual Exam score convention.

Wireless, Molecular, Graph, and BipedalWalker retain the archived task-specific mappings to a 0–100 scale. The public Borden and DABIC task configurations specify no separate rescaling. To combine them with the other Dual Exam tasks, we explicitly introduce

em,j=min⁡{100,max⁡{0,sm,jraw}},j∈{Borden,DABIC}.e_{m,j}=\min\{100,\max\{0,s^{\mathrm{raw}}_{m,j}\}\},\qquad j\in\{\mathrm{Borden},\mathrm{DABIC}\}.

This clipping is a Dual Exam aggregation convention, not an official EdgeBench normalization rule. It bounds each item’s contribution but does not establish equal task difficulty or make a score a success probability. Table 12 preserves the original values: Astra’s Borden score of 100.493 contributes 100 to the main table. Clipping does not explain why the raw score exceeds 100.

Budget and evidence.

We use the best recorded valid submission within an allowance of 43,200 seconds in the selected archived run, including valid submissions before early termination. This is our budget-limited aggregation, not a claim that every run completed the full EdgeBench horizon. Confirmed absence of a valid submission receives zero; a missing record is not automatically zero. The retained six configurations use their selected frozen run IDs. The additional four use the supplied result summary, with all four Wireless endpoints additionally checked against their best-submission judge reports. DeepSeek and MiMo Wireless stopped at model context/resume limits, but both passed 50/50 tests; their normalized scores are 19.9172 and 0, respectively. The latter is a mapped quality score, not missing-data imputation. MiniMax Wireless has conflicting checkpoint-validity and final pass-rate fields; either interpretation contributes zero under the mapping. The transferred trace archive is truncated, so the other added-task endpoints and evaluator-version equivalence have not all been independently verified. Astra uses a native Codex executor; these results compare model–harness configurations, not matched model-only capability.

Scope of the following workflow examples.

The following examples are organized by workflow behavior: selecting a tool, executing an extended procedure, and searching for an improved solution. This organization explains the recorded trajectories and is separate from the four subject-based categories used by the current scientific leaderboard. Counts and scores from the historical source collections are not current leaderboard denominators or results. These examples provide qualitative workflow illustrations rather than a representative sample of the 109 Scientific tasks.

A.14 Historical Workflow Example: Tool Selection

Tool selection tests whether an Agent chooses an appropriate next action from the task information already available. At each of ten derived checkpoints, evaluation checks the tool name, arguments, and number of calls against explicit requirements. Figure 18 shows why reading the identified source file is the appropriate next step before editing.

  • •

    T1: Reading the missing source context. The checkpoint identifies lines 410–505 of source/MACS3/Signal/PeakDetect.py as relevant to a code issue, but omits the surrounding changes in program state. It permits exactly one call and rules out another search or an immediate edit. GPT-5.6 Sol selects read_source with the specified file and line range. The accompanying figure presents a comparison of this response with the accepted tool, path, line bounds, and call count, all of which pass. The score of 1.0 assesses this decision only: the chosen tool is not executed, and the case contains no subsequent repair.

A.15 Historical Workflow Examples: Extended Execution

Long Horizon tasks test whether an Agent can carry a sequence of dependent actions through to a verifiable output. The historical collection contains 147 tasks from Agents’ Last Exam (ALE) and 30 scientific code-repair tasks from SWE. The two examples illustrate complementary workflows: producing and checking numerical results, and diagnosing a software defect before submitting a tested patch. Both workflows depend on intermediate checks to reach the final deliverable.

  • •

    L1: Ising computation from specification to evaluated files. The ALE task asks for a ten-qubit critical state, probabilities for all 1,024 measurement outcomes, site-1 density matrices, and one-body correlators. Figure 19 follows the evaluated Agent from reading the numerical specification to generating and checking four output files. It chooses exact diagonalization, then resolves a missing SciPy dependency by replacing an unsupported Python 3.14.3 environment with the available Python 3.10 interpreter. The successful return reports an eigenvector residual of 8.093×10−138.093\times 10^{-13} and probabilities summing to one.

    A second calculation using imaginary-time evolution produces observable differences below 5.71×10−45.71\times 10^{-4}, within the public tolerance of 10−210^{-2}. These checks support retaining the generated arrays, and the separately recorded evaluation assigns 1.0 to the final files. The comparison shares helper code with the generator, so it is a consistency check rather than an independent replication. The source archive identifies Codex as the execution framework, records the alias kindle-alpha-api, and groups the run under the model label gpt-5-6-sol.

  • •

    L2: Propagating a tuned parameter into a DFT calculation. The code-repair task concerns a density-functional theory calculation whose tuned parameter does not affect the result. Figure 20 shows that pbe_xc(omega) receives the parameter but returns the same PBE functional regardless of its value. The baseline therefore reports identical energies despite a tuned value near 0.67137. The Agent checks PySCF syntax, updates the function to use the parameter and reject invalid values, and fixes an import error in its verification script.

    The rerun returns different functional strings and an energy difference of approximately −0.34018629-0.34018629 Hartree. The submitted patch receives reward 1 with all three verifier tests passing. This demonstrates that the parameter now affects the calculation; it does not establish that one functional is more physically accurate than another. The recorded GPT-5.6 Sol run uses Claude Code; the figure separates its checks from the external verifier.

Appendix B Details of World Model Evaluation

This appendix illustrates how World Models are evaluated under fixed action instructions. The six cases cover scientific, social, physical, and digital settings, with checks for requested action effects, preservation of objects and participants, coordination, and adherence to changing rules. Figures 21–26 use six shared checkpoints per case: columns identify the same instructed step across models, while each row follows one model through the selected states. The reference image defines the starting scene, rather than a complete ground-truth trajectory.

The first four rows show image models, separated from eleven video models by a horizontal line. The first four cases use Seedream 5.0 Pro, while the two interface cases use Seedream 5.0. The panels retain the selected source runs, including the physical Yume runs_hard_v2 batch, the pendulum and mentorship yume-5b runs, and September 2026 Kling reruns. Generation histories and evaluation rubrics differ across packages, and the interface cases were preselected upstream; these panels illustrate behavior without supporting a controlled model ranking.

Modalities and comparability.

Image and video configurations provide different temporal evidence. Both can be checked for visible identity, object state, and requested changes at matched checkpoints, whereas properties such as an oscillation period require temporally resolved outputs. The modality, supplied history, intervention duration, and applicable checks must therefore accompany each configuration’s results. A static checkpoint does not establish a temporal property. The illustrative panels separate image and video models, but historical runs with different histories or rubrics do not constitute a controlled cross-model comparison. They should be interpreted independently of the full-coverage aggregate ranking unless their provenance matches the current evaluation protocol.

Rule changes: single pendulum.

Figure 21 tests whether a model preserves the apparatus while responding to a change in gravity. After release and a push, step 4 replaces Earth gravity with lunar gravity without requesting physical motion at that step. Steps 5 and 6 then request continued evolution under the new rule, and step 7 restores the original view. The copper bob, thin rod, and black support should remain identifiable throughout. Some displayed sequences instead alter or lose parts of the apparatus; for example, Alaya’s final view no longer depicts the original pendulum. Static checkpoints can reveal such changes, but verifying the specified oscillation period requires the video. For Yume, the archived step-4 image is inherited from the previous state. It should therefore be interpreted as a carried-forward checkpoint, rather than new visual evidence of the evaluated model’s response to the gravity change.

Participant-specific actions: painting-studio mentorship.

Figure 22 tests whether changes are applied to the named participant while other attributes remain stable. A is the standing mentor and B the seated student. After a neutral baseline and restored view, A looks toward B and raises one hand; B later responds with a small nod. At step 9, A should lower only the hand while retaining the gaze toward B. The figure panels therefore support checks of identity, pose, and scene continuity. Changes in framing or appearance, visible in several rows, can make these checks difficult even when the generated image remains plausible. The selected states do not establish the timing of the student’s response within a video.

Coordinated actions: dual-arm cup manipulation.

Figure 23 begins with two robot arms and three cups. The instructions require concurrent movements, resolution of competing nesting actions, a hand-over, a role exchange, an action by only one arm, and final withdrawal. Evaluation checks whether cup identities and orientations remain consistent and whether each arm realizes its assigned action. For example, the role change at step 7 must carry forward into step 8, when the right arm waits. The EchoWM and Yume rows visibly introduce human hands, illustrating an identity change that is distinct from an incorrect cup arrangement. End-state images can show these discrepancies, but cannot establish the order of actions within a step or whether an arm remained stationary throughout the sequence it.

Memory across interventions: dual trays.

Figure 24 samples a 20-step task whose standing goal is to bring a glass jar to the blue tray and align both trays. The model must retain intermediate states while tray rules, arm roles, and camera views change. Steps 7 and 10 bracket a visit to another bench and therefore test whether returning to the first bench recovers its established state. Steps 5 and 18 change rules without requesting immediate motion. Several displayed sequences instead change tray appearance or leave the original workspace; Yume’s final checkpoint, for example, shows a wooden bench. The final state must still be checked against the standing goal; its presence alone does not certify completion.

Local actions and persistent state: Minesweeper.

Figure 25 tests whether a model updates specified cells while preserving the rest of the board. The selected steps flag g1 and i1, reveal e5, and then flag g2, h2, and i2; the omitted step 2 flags h1. A correct sequence must retain earlier flags and avoid changing unrelated cells or the board layout. The figure panels show failures ranging from altered board geometry to replacement of the interface; LingBot, for example, produces a different graphic rather than the original grid. A visually stable board still requires cell-level inspection to establish that the requested changes occurred, so preservation of the overall layout alone is insufficient evidence of success.

Search and filtering: Google Shopping.

Figure 26 follows six instructions: enter Google Pixel 7, select the query, enable Buy on Google, select 128 GB and Snow, and open the sorting menu. Earlier task values must persist, unrelated interface regions must remain unchanged, and an action is permitted only when its target is visible and usable. The panels therefore test both the requested update and continuity of the surrounding page. Some rows retain much of the starting layout, while others alter the interface substantially; Minimax eventually replaces the shopping page with a dialog. These examples illustrate why readable product imagery alone does not establish correct search, filtering, or preservation of prior selections.

Appendix C Execution Provenance and Evidence Boundaries

Reference conditions and validation coverage.

A fixed reference mechanism supplies repeatable task rules, not a guarantee of an error-free environment. The collection includes scene and route tasks with reference constraints, software interaction with task-specific verification, rule-governed social scenarios, and scientific workflows checked by their original verifiers. The added SWE tasks use executable tests; ToolChoice uses a strict decision-checkpoint schema. These evidence types support different claims: a test pass certifies the tested behavior, while an observation or task score does not establish every latent property. We do not have a unified, independent error audit across all reference environments. Neither case-construction screening nor expert review of specifications supplies an agreement estimate for scores assigned to generated outputs. Unreported audit coverage must not be interpreted as zero reference error.

Scientific configuration identifiers.

The added-task records identify the configurations as gpt-6-astra, gpt-5.6-sol, gemini-3.6-flash, qwen3.8-max, kimi-k3, deepseek-v4.1-flash, glm-5.3-flash, doubao-seed-2-1-pro-260628, MiniMax-M3, and mimo-v2.5. These identifiers do not recover immutable provider versions or imply the same harness across the other benchmark families. The historical examples retain their recorded configurations and are not evidence of switching models inside the fixed-pair pilot. Source differences among historical WM illustrations are documented in Appendix B.

Exclusions and retained failures in the added tasks.

The retained six-configuration SWE collection contains 180 accepted records. Infrastructure replacements were used for failed executions; excluded-attempt totals for the retained subset are not separately consolidated. In contrast, observable model or harness behavior remains in the accepted scores: all 30 Seed runs produced thinking without task tools, and 26 Kimi runs had interrupted tool execution. These zeros describe the evaluated configuration, not an isolated estimate of the base model’s reasoning ability. The four-configuration extension retains 29 reported timeouts (GLM 14, DeepSeek one, MiMo ten, Astra four) and one Astra tool-cap termination as scored outcomes; its report lists no verifier errors. These audit facts do not determine invalid-run rates for the rest of the benchmark.

Known scoring and provenance limitations.

Six added ToolChoice checkpoints require a task_id argument that was not supplied in their prompts. We retain the original strict scores for traceability and disclose this schema/prompt mismatch; a corrected prompt would define a revised evaluation requiring consistent rescoring. One repair-task title differs from its recorded instruction, although both retain the same Physical Sciences reporting assignment. The local task mapping does not preserve upstream SWE-bench instance identifiers, so the stated SWE-bench provenance is not yet a complete reproducible source manifest. Task-source counts and scientific scores appear in Tables 10 and 11.

Response, repair, progress, and completion.

A corrective response is an observable targeted action after an eligible discrepancy. A successful repair additionally requires subsequent evidence that the discrepancy was resolved. Partial progress describes satisfied intermediate requirements; strict task success requires the complete goal and all constraints. We do not infer successful repair from response counts. The pilot’s Social corrective-response value of 25% is an average of case-level eligible-event fractions, whereas its 0% task-success value counts fully successful cases; they use different denominators and measure different events. Zero strict success is compatible with local progress. Existing graded task scores remain task-specific; no new, post-hoc partial-credit metric is introduced here.

Audit and uncertainty still needed.

No independent stratified WM score agreement, repeated-run confidence interval, or full invalid-run audit is reported. A reproducible audit should bind each case identifier to its source, frozen specification, rubric and verifier version, configuration, attempts, raw trace, score, and exclusion reason. An independent sample should span scenarios and output modalities, report sample size and ambiguous checks, and record disagreements before adjudication. Resampling must account for shared Social templates and SWE/ToolChoice parent links. The present across-configuration standard deviations and equal-domain sensitivity analysis are not substitutes for that evidence.

Appendix D Preliminary Study Protocol and Packing-Case Diagnostics

Study configuration.

The preliminary study uses the same model pairing throughout: GPT-5.6 Sol selects actions, and Seedance 2.5 generates the resulting observations. The 150 cases are evenly distributed across Minecraft, Daily Life, Embodied Tasks, Web UI, Driving, Desktop Software, Industrial Systems, Natural Ecosystems, Scientific Experiments, and Social Interaction, with 15 cases per scenario.

Excluded runs.

Initialization failures and technical failures are excluded from the reported 150 cases and from the task-success denominator; they are not counted as task failures. The reported 0% success rate therefore corresponds to zero successes among the 150 included cases, rather than among all attempted runs.

Interaction budget.

Each case is run once, with a maximum of 20 interaction steps and no episode-level retries. Repeating or revising an action within the ongoing trajectory is distinct from restarting a case and consumes the same step budget. The navigation retries discussed below are such within-trajectory actions, not additional evaluation attempts.

Response versus repair.

Agent Corrective Response records a targeted action following a visible discrepancy, not whether that action restores the required state. Successful repair would require separate evidence from subsequent observations that the same discrepancy has been resolved; task success additionally requires the complete goal and all constraints. Thus the 25.0% response rate for Social Interaction is a case-averaged behavioral rate, not a repair-success rate or the fraction of successful tasks. It cannot be converted into event counts without the underlying case-level denominators. Differences in discrepancy types and response opportunities also prevent interpreting a higher response rate as stronger recovery ability. The current aggregate results do not establish which responses produce repairs, and response behavior alone is insufficient as an optimization objective: ineffective responses may still receive credit. Evaluating repair outcomes and checking credited responses against the original discrepancies are needed to assess this risk.

Evidence and scope.

Figure 2(b) uses one recorded 14-step GPT-5.6 Sol–Seedance 2.5 rollout, not an aggregate over the preliminary collection. The six displayed frames are from steps 1, 3, 6, 8, 12, and 14; the curves use all 14 recorded steps. The task specifies a burgundy passport with a gold band, a red medicine case with a white cross, and a white charger with an orange cable, all packed into the same blue backpack with a yellow star. A single automated retrospective review inspected eight frames per four-second segment at 2 fps, together with the initialization image and selected full-resolution tail frames. The labels have not been independently adjudicated, and the rubric was specified after inspecting the case. The offline failure assessment rests on the use of a different blue pouch for later packing and carrying, rather than on an assumption that occluded items are missing; it does not certify completion of the original runner’s technical validation.

Checks and response windows.

Each step is assessed for original-backpack identity, persistence of visibly acquired items, and task-conditioned action results. Of 42 candidate checks, 6 pass, 13 fail, 22 are unknown, and 1 is inapplicable. Unknown and inapplicable checks are excluded, giving an assessable coverage of 19/4119/41 and a World State Consistency score of 6/196/19. For Agent Corrective Response, a qualifying response is targeted verification, reselection, replanning, or a retry within the next two actions after a visible discrepancy available to the MA. A persistent identity discrepancy is counted once; an event with only one subsequent action is excluded. Two of seven eligible events receive a response, both navigation retries. A retry does not establish successful repair.

Curve construction.

Let FtF_{t} count failed state checks through step tt, and let MtM_{t} count eligible discrepancies whose complete two-action windows have ended without a corrective response. The plotted retained scores for World State Consistency (StS_{t}) and Agent Corrective Response (RtR_{t}) are

St=1−Ft19,Rt=1−Mt7.S_{t}=1-\frac{F_{t}}{19},\qquad R_{t}=1-\frac{M_{t}}{7}.

Both denominators are fixed using the complete trajectory. Failures contribute one deduction each at steps 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 9, and 11, and two each at steps 12–14. Missed-response deductions occur at steps 3, 8, 10, 13, and 14, when the corresponding windows close. Thus S14=6/19S_{14}=6/19 and R14=2/7R_{14}=2/7. Unknown checks incur no deductions and are not labeled successful. Each score remains unchanged unless its corresponding failure or missed response is newly counted. Straight segments connect integer-step values only as visual guides.

Interpretation and sensitivity.

The initial value of 1 is assigned, not measured: initialization already deviates from the specification, and the wrong-colored passport is visible at step 1. Monotonicity follows from cumulative deductions and does not demonstrate monotonic degradation of either model’s capability. Navigation checks use arrival inside the requested room by segment end. Treating doorway-only outcomes at steps 4 and 11 as unknown and excluding their response events changes the final rates to 6/17=0.3536/17=0.353 and 1/5=0.2001/5=0.200. The absence of responses to the four identity discrepancies and the final wrong-container failure are unchanged.
